name: San José Central Market
label: Central Market
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/264040874: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Mercado Central de San José' (129 m across).
notes: A lively covered market with food stalls, coffee, and souvenirs.

text.description:
San José Central Market is the city's largest market, and it fills an entire block on Avenida Central. It opened in 1880 and is still a busy working place rather than a showpiece. Inside is a maze of narrow alleys with more than 200 shops, stalls and small, inexpensive restaurants called sodas. You'll find meat, fish, fruit, vegetables, coffee, flowers, herbal remedies, souvenirs and local handcrafts, and even snakeskin boots and cowboy saddles. Tens of thousands of people pass through each day.

That mix is what makes it good for photos. Every few steps there is a new scene: piles of colourful produce, hanging goods, hand-painted signs, cooks at counters and shoppers moving through tight lanes. Keep your phone in your hand and your bag zipped, because the alleys are crowded and you'll want to move easily.

Look for repeating patterns, such as rows of stalls, strings of goods or stacked fruit, and shoot along an alley for depth. For close-ups, choose a single stall or product and fill the frame. If you want to photograph a person, smile and ask first. Mercado Borbón, which specialises in food, is two blocks to the north if you want a second stop.
text.geographic_location: The market sits in central San José on Avenida Central, taking up a whole city block about 250 m northwest of the Parque Central.
text.directions_text: The market is about 250 m northwest of the Parque Central, so head in that direction from the park. If you are coming from further away, check a local map for the best way to reach Avenida Central, then walk the last stretch. The phone icon on the map is about 10 m east of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the narrow alleys and busy crossings, and the default lens (1x) for most stalls and people. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as fruit, coffee or crafts without leaning over the counter.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 10 m east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. From here, walk the nearest alleys and shoot along them rather than staying in one spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up an alley along a vertical line so the rows of stalls lead the eye into the picture. Fill the frame with one stall or product for close-ups. Use portrait mode for a stallholder or a food counter, once they have agreed to be photographed.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on your subject, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so bright openings and signs don't wash out. If the light is dim in the alleys, hold the phone steady for a moment and let night mode work if it switches on.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the market is open and busy so the stalls are full, but expect crowds. Ask locally or check a current map listing for opening hours before you go.

text.access_note: This is a working public market, but opening times and any rules on photography may change, so ask locally or check a current map listing before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Asking permission before photographing stallholders is polite and often welcome.
The alleys are crowded, so pickpocketing is possible and bags should be kept closed.
Lighting inside the alleys can be dim in places, so night mode may trigger.
The market is livelier and its stalls fuller when it is busy during its open hours.

name: Metropolitan Cathedral of San José
label: Metropolitan Cathedral
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/264042444: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Catedral Metropolitana de San José' (97 m across).
notes: The main church of the capital stands on the east side of Parque Central.

text.description:
The Metropolitan Cathedral is a cathedral in San José, standing in the city centre on Calle Central, by Avenues 2 and 4. The first cathedral here was built in 1802 but was destroyed by an earthquake. That history is worth a line in your photo caption.

It photographs well because it is a large, solid civic landmark in the middle of a busy city. You can shoot it as a whole building, or step closer and pick out details such as the doorway, the stonework and the people passing in front. Including a few passers-by gives a sense of scale and shows it is a working part of city life, not just a monument.

The phone icon on the map is about 25 m south of the subject. From there you can fit a good part of the building into one frame without tilting your phone steeply upwards. Keep the phone level, use the gridlines to keep vertical edges straight, and take a few steps left or right to avoid street signs and parked vehicles. If you want a closer detail shot, walk up to the building and zoom rather than cropping later. Check the official site before you go if you plan to look inside, as visiting arrangements may change.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of San José, Costa Rica, on Calle Central, by Avenues 2 and 4.
text.directions_text: Head for the cathedral on Calle Central, by Avenues 2 and 4, in the centre of San José. Ask for the Catedral Metropolitana if you need directions. The phone icon on the map is about 25 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole front of the building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are too close or want to include more of the street. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the doorway or stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 25 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. This gives you room to fit most of it in the frame without tilting the phone steeply.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the building with them so the walls stay upright. Put the cathedral in the centre or slightly to one side. Include a little foreground, such as pavement or people walking by, to give a sense of scale. For a tighter second shot, walk closer and zoom in on one detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Make sure the phone is held level, as tilting it upwards makes the walls lean inwards. In dim light, night mode works well if you can hold the phone steady against something.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows. Midday sun can be strong, so check the exposure.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street, but as a place of worship it may have visiting rules for the inside, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The cathedral can be seen and photographed from the street outside.
It is a working place of worship and may have visiting rules for the interior.
Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer than midday light.
Passers-by, street signs and parked vehicles may appear in the frame near the cathedral.

name: Museo del Jade
label: Jade Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: The world's largest collection of American jade.

text.description:
The Museo del Jade is an archaeological museum in San José, facing Plaza de la Democracia. For a phone photographer it works best as a subject in its own right: a solid, modern building with an open square in front of it, so you can step back and fit the whole frontage into one shot without much trouble. The plaza also gives you room to move left and right until the lines of the building look tidy and level.

A few facts help to set the scene. The museum was founded in 1977 by Fidel Tristán Castro, the first president of the INS, and it moved to its present home in front of the plaza in 2014. It holds what is described as the world's largest collection of American jade, which is a good thing to mention in a caption alongside your photo.

For practical photo advice, start with a wide view of the building from the open space in front of it, then move closer for details such as the entrance and any signs or textures that catch your eye. Turn on the gridlines so the vertical edges of the building stay straight, and tap on the building to set focus and brightness. People often wander through the plaza, so take a few frames and pick the one with the cleanest foreground. Photography inside a museum is often limited, so check the official site before you go if you hope to take pictures of the displays.
text.geographic_location: The Museo del Jade is in San José, facing Plaza de la Democracia.
text.directions_text: Head for Plaza de la Democracia in San José. The phone icon on the map is about 370 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole frontage in from close range, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural-looking view. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for picking out details on the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 370 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. To fit the full frontage in, move back from the building until the whole frontage sits comfortably in the frame, then face the museum.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line up the edges of the building with the vertical lines so it does not lean. Keep the phone level, and try one shot with a little foreground from the plaza and one close-up of the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out. If you have to stand close, the ultra-wide (0.5x) can stretch the edges, so keep the building away from the corners of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in daylight, when the building is evenly lit. Quieter moments in the plaza make it easier to get a clear foreground.

text.access_note: Check the museum's official site for entry rules before you go; the plaza in front is the open space for outside photos.

name: National Theatre of Costa Rica
label: Teatro Nacional
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24857113: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Teatro Nacional' (86 m across).
notes: The neoclassical 1897 theatre is the cultural symbol of the capital.

text.description:
The National Theatre of Costa Rica (Teatro Nacional) is the country's national theatre, in the central part of San José. It opened on 21 October 1897 with a performance of Goethe's Faust, and it holds 1,140 people. It was paid for in part by a tax on coffee, then the country's main export, and the building is often called the finest historic building in the capital. That makes it a rewarding subject even if you never go inside.

From outside, the front is the main attraction. Statues of the playwright Calderón de la Barca and the composer Ludwig van Beethoven stand on the façade, and there are further monuments by the entrance walkway, including one of Chopin. These give you small details to photograph as well as the whole building. Inside, the theatre is known for its lavish furnishings and for the mural Allegory of Coffee and Bananas by Aleardo Villa, which also appears on the five colón bill.

The theatre is still a working venue. It has performances several times a week, including the National Symphonic Orchestra's regular season, and it also welcomes visitors. Shoot the full façade first, then move closer for the statues and the entrance. If you go inside, the mural and the decorated interior are the pictures to look for. Photography rules inside can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The theatre is in the central section of San José.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot. The theatre is in the central section of San José. From there the theatre is 66 m to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 25 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole façade, because you are close to a large building. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statues and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 25 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the building parallel to the edge of the screen, holding the phone upright and level so the walls do not lean. Take one wide shot of the whole building, then a closer one of the statues at the front. A few steps to either side will give you a cleaner view of the entrance walkway and its monuments.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the façade to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the stonework and sky keep their detail. If you go inside, tap on the mural and raise the exposure slightly, as indoor light is dim. Tap-to-focus also helps with the statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the façade. If you want a night shot, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on something steady while it captures.

text.access_note: The theatre is a working venue and visitor attraction, so access to the inside may be ticketed or restricted; check the official site before you go.

Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer on a building façade.

name: Plaza de la Cultura
label: Plaza de la Cultura
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Teatro Nacional' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Teatro Nacional' (way/24857113): middle (86 m across); moved 20 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM R6275464 (Plaza de la Cultura): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The busy pedestrian square in front of the National Theatre.

text.description:
Plaza de la Cultura is a wide, paved public square in the middle of San José, with the Teatro Nacional on its edge. It is not a pretty garden. A guide describes it as a plain concrete space, so the pictures here come from people, street life and the theatre rather than the ground itself. That is also why it works for a phone: you can catch a candid scene, a busy crowd or a quiet moment without any set-up.

The best frame is from the steps in front of the Teatro Nacional, looking out over the plaza. The theatre's neoclassical facade fills the foreground, and the open square with its visitors spreads out beyond it. A travel blog recommends golden hour at the theatre steps. Be aware that the theatre is the main subject from the steps, and the plaza becomes the background.

For a second view, walk out into the plaza and look back for a wide shot across the paved space and its greenery and fountain, with the theatre rising at the edge of the frame. Another option is the entrance from Avenida Central, which gives a street-level scene with people passing. The square sits between Avenida Central and Avenida Segunda, between calles 3 and 5. Reviews say it gets crowded at weekends and at peak hours, so go at a quieter time if you want a clear view of the facade. If you want people in the picture, a busy moment suits you better.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of San José, on the square between Avenida Central and Avenida Segunda, between calles 3 and 5. The Teatro Nacional stands on its edge.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so it is reached on foot or by road in central San José. Head for the block between Avenida Central and Avenida Segunda, between calles 3 and 5, where the Teatro Nacional stands on the edge of the plaza. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade and plaza in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the theatre. Use 2x telephoto, if your phone has it, for people and small scenes across the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Teatro Nacional (steps in front of the theatre, facing the plaza). The theatre's neoclassical facade in the foreground, with the open plaza and its visitors spread out beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the facade's vertical lines straight, holding the phone level so the building does not lean. Put the theatre in the foreground and let people in the plaza fill the space behind it. For an alternative, walk into the plaza and look back for a wide view with the theatre at the edge of the frame, or shoot from the Avenida Central entrance for a street-level scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail. Live Photos can catch the movement of people crossing the plaza.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, which a travel blog recommends at the theatre steps. Off-peak hours are likely to be quieter than weekends.

text.access_note: Reviews note that the plaza gets crowded at weekends and at peak hours, so allow for people in your frame.

name: Spirogyra Butterfly Farm Park Garden
label: Spirogyra Butterflies
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Spirogyra Butterfly Farm Park Garden' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q28311036: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: A butterfly garden near the city centre.

text.description:
Spirogyra is a small butterfly house in Barrio Amón, San José. Inside a climate-controlled, glass-enclosed space, roughly 50 to 60 species of live butterflies from around Costa Rica fly among flowering plants, trees and cascading waterfalls. A few free-flying birds share the space, and there is a learning centre where you can see caterpillars feeding on their host plants.

It photographs well because everything is close and colourful. The butterflies settle on flowers, so you can get near without chasing them. The waterfalls and greenery give you a backdrop for wider scenes. Species on display include the blue Morpho peleides, the large owl butterflies (Caligo) and the zebra heliconian, so there is plenty to look for. Move slowly, wait for a butterfly to land, and let it come to you rather than reaching toward it.

The best pictures are taken inside, among the flowering plants and the waterfall area, so this is a paid view. Before you go, check the official site for admission, opening hours and any rules or fees for photography. From the street, the green, plant-filled frontage of the small house also makes a pleasant outside shot of the place.
text.geographic_location: In Barrio Amón, in the Carmen District of San José, on the edge of the Río Torres and just north of Zoológico Simón Bolívar.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot. The garden lies north of Zoológico Simón Bolívar, on the edge of the Río Torres, so use the zoo as a landmark and head north towards the river. You can also look up its Spanish name, Mariposario Spirogyra, in your maps app. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most shots of flowers, butterflies and the waterfall. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole waterfall scene, and to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for butterflies that land out of reach.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Inside the garden, stand among the flowering plants and near the waterfall area. From there you can frame butterflies on the flowers with the waterfall set in the glass enclosure behind them. As a second option, take a street-level shot of the entrance and the green frontage of the small house.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: For close-ups, wait for a butterfly to settle on a flower, then fill the frame with it and leave a little space around the wings. For a wider scene, use the waterfall and plants as a backdrop. Turn on gridlines to keep the picture level, and use the entrance frontage as an alternative outside shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the butterfly to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so bright wings and sky do not wash out. Try portrait mode on a butterfly that sits still. Live Photos can catch a wing-flutter, and the telephoto lets you keep your distance. Wipe the lens first, since glass-enclosed, humid spaces can leave it misty.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the garden is open and check the official site for current hours. Bright daytime hours suit butterflies, but a quieter visit makes it easier to frame your shots.

text.access_note: This is a paid, ticketed garden, so check the official site before you go for admission, opening hours and any photography rules or fees.

notes: The largest city park, with a lake, sports fields, and walking paths.

text.description: La Sabana is the largest urban park in Costa Rica and is often called "the lungs of San José". It covers about 0.72 square kilometres of lawns, trees and sports grounds right beside the city's core districts, so it makes a good break from street photography. The park was officially inaugurated in 1977, though the land has been used for recreation for about two centuries. In 2001 it was declared National Architectural Heritage. Two buildings stand out. One is the national stadium. The other is the Costa Rican Museum of Art, which occupies the former main building of the old La Sabana Airport. There is also a large artificial lake, plus running and skating tracks and several sports fields. For photos, look for wide, open scenes: grass and trees in the foreground, with a building or the lake behind. People jogging, skating or playing sport add life and scale to a picture. The park is big, so choose one view and take your time rather than trying to cover it all. Keep your lens clean, because a quick wipe makes a visible difference outdoors. Photograph the museum and stadium from the open grass rather than close up, so the whole building fits in the frame. If you want a change from wide views, take a few close shots of the trees and park life.
text.geographic_location: La Sabana Metropolitan Park is in downtown San José, next to the city's core districts. Several institutions have their main offices around its edge.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so make your own way to La Sabana park from downtown San José. From there the subject lies about 400 m to the south-west, which is about 5 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 410 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the open lawns and big sky, and switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of buildings and people. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a detail such as the stadium or a runner on the track.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 410 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line. Use a tree, a path or the lake edge as a foreground to give depth. Keep the phone level so buildings do not lean. If you can, include a person walking or jogging for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main subject to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the clouds keep their detail. Try panorama mode for the wide open grounds, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the grass. Midday sun is bright and flat.

text.access_note: The park is a large public green space, but individual buildings such as the museum or stadium may have their own access rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Costa Rican Museum of Art
label: Museum of Art
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/38934051: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museum of Costa Rican Art' (67 m across).
notes: Housed in the former airport terminal, with a relief-covered facade.

text.description:
The Costa Rican Museum of Art (Museo de Arte Costarricense, or MAC) sits in a building with a past that surprises many visitors: it was once the terminal of La Sabana airport. Building began in 1937 and the terminal opened in 1940. After the airport closed in 1974, the land became part of La Sabana Metropolitan Park, and the old terminal opened as an art museum on 3 May 1978. In 1986 it was named architectural heritage of Costa Rica, and it reopened in October 2011 after a renovation.

That history is what makes it a good photo stop. You are photographing a former airport building that is now a museum, with parkland around it, so the whole building can be your subject without anything else crowding the frame. The outline is about 67 m across, so you will need to step back or use a wide view to fit it in.

Inside, the collection holds over 6000 works, though only about 150 can be shown at a time. One highlight is Francisco Amighetti's 1948 mural Agriculture, which commemorates the Costa Rican Civil War. Photo rules inside can differ from those outside, so ask staff before you shoot in the galleries.

For the outside, take a few frames from different distances: one wide shot of the whole building, one closer shot of the entrance or a detail of the façade, and one with some park greenery in the foreground. Keep your phone level so the long lines of the building stay straight.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in La Sabana Metropolitan Park in San José, in the old La Sabana airport terminal building.
text.directions_text: Head for La Sabana Metropolitan Park in San José and look for the former airport terminal that now houses the museum. No station or tram stop is listed nearby. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because you will be close to a building about 67 m across. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the entrance or the façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face south for the main view, then move away from the building across the park until the whole of it fits in your frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the roofline so the horizontals stay level. Use the ultra-wide from close up and keep the phone upright to limit leaning verticals. For a second frame, step back, use the default lens (1x) and include a strip of park greenery along the bottom.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its colour and the sky is not washed out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the façade than the middle of the day. Check the museum's opening days before you go.

text.access_note: The grounds are part of a public park, but entry to the museum itself may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Museo Nacional de Costa Rica
label: National Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de la Democracia y de la Abolición del Ejército' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de la Democracia y de la Abolición del Ejército' (way/318884308): middle (139 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4144800: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museo Nacional de Costa Rica' (148 m across).
notes: Set in the old Bellavista Fortress, with butterfly garden and bullet-scarred walls.

text.description: The Museo Nacional de Costa Rica fills a yellow, fortress-like building with turrets, which is why it photographs so well from across the open plaza. It was built in 1917 as the Bellavista barracks and housed soldiers. It was also caught up in the Costa Rican Civil War of 1948. The museum moved into this building in 1950, and it looks the part, with solid walls, towers and a good deal of sky around them. The best open-air view is from the Plaza de la Democracia y de la Abolición del Ejército, looking across the tiered concrete steps to the museum's west facade. Statues dotted around the square make useful foreground details, and the plaza is generally quieter than many city squares. Start with the whole building in the frame, then move in for towers, windows and statues. A closer frontal shot of the facade is a good second picture if you walk over to the museum itself. Inside, the museum holds historical documents and national treasures. Photography rules indoors can change, so check at the entrance. The pre-Columbian room has been reported closed for remodelling, so check before you go if that is your main reason for visiting.
text.geographic_location: In central San José, on Calle 17 between Avenida Central and Avenida Segunda, in the Cuesta de Moras area. The museum sits right beside the Plaza de la Democracia.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so simply head for the Plaza de la Democracia in central San José. The museum is on Avenida Central at Calle 17, beside the plaza. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the full facade from across the plaza. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the steps and statues large in the foreground, and keep the building's edges away from the corners of the frame to limit stretching. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the turrets and details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de la Democracia y de la Abolición del Ejército (across the plaza from the museum's west facade). The yellow former Bellavista barracks fronting the tiered concrete plaza, with its turrets and the statues scattered across the square in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the building's verticals straight by holding your phone level. Put the facade along the upper third and let the plaza steps lead the eye towards it. Wait for a statue to sit on one side as a foreground detail. For a different picture, walk to the museum itself for a closer frontal shot of the fortress-like facade and its towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the yellow wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks washed out. This keeps the colour of the building rich.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is likely to suit the west-facing facade best, with softer, warmer light on the yellow walls. Mornings can leave it in shade.

text.access_note: The plaza is an open public square. Check the museum's official site for entry details, indoor photography rules and which rooms are open.

name: Pre-Columbian Gold Museum
label: Gold Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/459837504: the OpenStreetMap point 'Museo del Oro Precolombino'.
notes: Thousands of golden pre-Columbian objects are displayed under Plaza de la Cultura.

text.description: The Pre-Columbian Gold Museum sits underneath the Plaza de la Cultura, so there is no grand building to photograph. What you see is an open city square, with the museum tucked below it. That makes this a spot for a scene-setting photo: the plaza, the people crossing it and the sense of a museum hidden under your feet. It is owned and curated by the Banco Central de Costa Rica. The collection holds 3,567 Pre-Columbian objects, including 1,586 gold pieces. The gold dates from around 300 to 400 BC up to 1550 AD. Among the displays are small gold animals such as frogs, eagles and jaguars, and a life-size gold warrior figure in a glass case. The same building also houses a coin museum, which includes Costa Rica's first coin, minted in 1825. For a good plaza shot, stand back far enough to include the open space and some sky, and wait for a gap in the crowd so the foreground is not cluttered. Add a person walking through for a sense of scale. Take a few frames at different times, as the square changes with the crowds. If you plan to go inside, check the official site before you go for the rules on taking photographs in the galleries.
text.geographic_location: In San José, Costa Rica, underneath the Plaza de la Cultura. The museum is in a subterranean building below the square.
text.directions_text: Head for the Plaza de la Cultura in San José; the museum is below the square. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so the plaza itself is the place to aim for. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the plaza. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to fit in more of the square and the sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as people crossing the plaza.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take your first photo here, then step back a few paces for a wider view of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower third line, depending on whether the sky or the plaza is more interesting that day. Include a person or two for scale. Keep your phone level so the buildings do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the screen on the brightest part of the scene to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky looks washed out. Try a Live Photo to catch people moving across the square, and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the plaza is quieter, so you get clear space in the foreground. Soft daylight is kinder than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The plaza is a public square, but the museum below is a managed attraction, so check the official site before you go for entry and photography rules.

name: Plaza de la Democracia
label: Plaza Democracia
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Museo Nacional de Costa Rica' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Museo Nacional de Costa Rica' (relation/4144800): middle (148 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q19385415: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: A wide plaza with crafts stalls, beside the National Museum.

text.description:
Plaza de la Democracia is a broad public square in the centre of San José, set directly in front of the building where Costa Rica's Legislative Assembly meets. The National Museum stands on one side and the Jade Museum on the other. That makes it a good place for a wide, open photo that says plainly 'this is the capital'.

The plaza opened in 1989 to mark 100 years since President Bernardo Soto Alfaro stepped aside rather than fight violently over his defeat in the 1889 election. It took its longer name, which adds the abolition of the army, in 2016. The army was abolished in 1948, and that event also took place here.

The classic picture is taken from the front of the National Museum, looking across the plaza. From there you can fit in the spherical structure holding a Diquís stone sphere on one side, the Figueres monument on the other, and the Jade Museum behind. If you want a second angle, the front of the Jade Museum gives a general view of the whole plaza with the National Museum in the background.

Keep the phone level so the buildings don't lean. Wait a moment for people to move out of the middle of the frame, or use them to show the size of the space. The plaza can be busy when events are on, and some visitors prefer to take care here in the evenings, so don't linger with your phone out once it gets dark.
text.geographic_location: In central San José, directly in front of the national congress building. The National Museum and the Jade Museum stand on either side of the plaza.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop serves this spot, so start from the centre of San José and make your way to the Museo Nacional de Costa Rica. From there the middle of the plaza lies to the west, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the plaza, both sides and the Jade Museum into one frame. If it feels too stretched, switch to the default lens (1x) and use panorama mode instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Museo Nacional de Costa Rica (front area facing the plaza, looking across it). A panoramic view across the plaza, with the spherical structure holding a Diquís stone sphere on one side, the Figueres monument on the other, and the Jade Museum in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the horizon and building edges with them so nothing tilts. Place the stone-sphere structure and the monument on either side of the frame and let the open paved space lead the eye to the Jade Museum. For an alternative view, try the front of the Jade Museum, looking back at the whole plaza with the National Museum behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mid-bright part of the buildings to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks washed out. For a panorama, move slowly and keep the phone upright. Wait for people to walk out of shot before you start.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the buildings. Aim for daytime, as the plaza can be less comfortable in the evening.

text.access_note: The plaza is an open public space; the museums beside it may have their own opening times and entry rules, so check the official sites before you go.

name: Parque Morazán
label: Parque Morazán
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Paseo de las Damas' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Hotel Paseo Las Damas' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM W31750857 (Parque Morazán): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: A historic park with the Templo de la Música pavilion.

text.description: Parque Morazán is a city park in San José, shaded by large trees and centred on the Templo de la Música, a neoclassical bandstand with columns and a dome. The park photographs well because the setting is so layered. The Paseo de las Damas, the avenue leading to the park, is a tree-lined walkway where the dama trees meet overhead to form a leafy canopy, with the Music Temple visible at the far end of the path. That gives you a ready-made frame. The trees make a natural border and the path leads the eye straight to the building. It is also a quieter, more composed picture than a head-on shot of the bandstand. Start on the Paseo de las Damas and take your time walking towards the park. Hold your phone level and use the gridlines to keep the path centred, so the trunks on either side look balanced. Then stroll on and photograph the Music Temple up close from the lawns around it, with the park's big trees behind and above it. Take a few frames at different heights: one at chest height for the whole scene, and one lower down to make the path seem longer. If people are walking along the path, wait a moment. A single figure in the distance adds scale, while a crowd can hide the bandstand.
text.geographic_location: Parque Morazán is a city park in San José, reached along the Paseo de las Damas, the tree-lined avenue that leads to it. The Templo de la Música stands within the park.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so get to the park by whatever local means suits you. The Paseo de las Damas, approached from the south, is a separate spot and is not where the icon sits. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the walkway and the Music Temple at the end. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the full canopy of branches overhead. Try the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pull the bandstand closer and make the path look more compressed.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Paseo de las Damas (approach from the south, the avenue leading to the park). A tree-lined walkway with the dama trees forming a canopy, with the Music Temple visible at the end of the path.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place yourself in the middle of the path so the trees line up on both sides and the Music Temple sits in the centre. Keep the phone straight so the trunks do not lean. For a different view, walk into the park and photograph the Templo de la Música up close from the lawns, with the large trees around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Music Temple to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the bright gap at the end of the path washes out. Under thick tree cover the light can be patchy, so check the shot before you move on.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sun is not directly overhead, such as morning or late afternoon, so the light under the trees is softer. A quieter moment also helps keep the path clear.

text.access_note: Parque Morazán is a public park. Check the official site for any closures or photo restrictions before you go.

name: Costa Rica National Stadium (2011)
label: Estadio Nacional
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).

notes: The national stadium, on the western edge of La Sabana Park.

text.description:
Costa Rica's National Stadium is a big, modern arena in La Sabana Metropolitan Park, San José. It was completed in early 2011 and opened to the public on 26 March that year. It holds around 42,000 seats and is the home ground of the national football team. It was the first modern sporting and events arena built in Central America, and it replaced the old National Stadium, which was demolished in 2008. China financed and built it, and about 800 Chinese workers came over for the job. That story is a good caption for your picture.

It photographs well because of its size and clean shape. A large curved roof and open park around it give you room to step back and fit a lot into the frame. With grass or sky around the building, the picture stays simple and uncluttered. Once you have the wide shot, try a closer one of the roofline or the big video screen in the southern section.

Take a few frames at different distances and keep the horizon level. On match or concert days the area can be busy, so expect people in your shots.
text.geographic_location: The stadium is in La Sabana Metropolitan Park, San José. It stands in the open parkland around it.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed nearby, so get to La Sabana Metropolitan Park by whatever local means you prefer. Once you are in the park, it is about 4 minutes on foot to the stadium itself. The phone icon on the map is about 55 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole stadium in with a bit of sky and park around it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you stand close and the roof is cut off. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the roofline and screen.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 55 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. From here the whole building sits in front of you with open ground between you and it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the base of the stadium on the lower line, leaving the roof and sky above. Keep the phone level so the curved roof does not lean. For a second picture, zoom in on the roof edge or the screen. People walking in the park make good scale for a final shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stadium to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. If the roof looks too dark, nudge exposure up instead. Try panorama only if you are close, and move slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the roof than midday. Go on a quiet day if you want the park empty.

text.access_note: The stadium stands in a public park, but entry to the stadium itself depends on events, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: The León Cortés Castro Monument is a tribute in San José, and it works well as a quick, easy phone stop. Treat the monument as your main subject, which suits a phone: you can show it large in the frame, then take a second, wider picture that includes the surrounding street or open space so the photo says where you were. Walk around it a little before you choose, because the background changes quickly with a few steps to either side. Look for a view where nothing awkward, such as a lamp post, sign or parked vehicle, appears to grow out of the top of the monument. Switch on the gridlines in your camera settings to keep verticals straight, and tap the monument on screen so the phone sets focus and brightness for it rather than for a bright sky. If the sky is washing out, drag the exposure slider down a touch. Take a few frames at different distances and keep the best. For the name on any plaque, a close-up photo is a handy record. Details such as the monument's date and history are not covered here, so read any plaque on site.
text.geographic_location: It stands in San José, Costa Rica. Find the León Cortés Castro Monument on the map to see the surrounding streets and the exact spot.
text.directions_text: The phone icon on the map is about 20 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the monument. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want to include more of the surroundings, and keep the monument away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched. The telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) is useful for a tighter shot of the monument's details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. You can also step a little closer for a tighter picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Place the monument slightly off-centre using the gridlines, and keep the vertical lines straight by holding the phone level. Take one close shot and one wider shot that shows the setting. Try a low position with the default lens (1x) for a stronger sense of height, but check that nothing is cut off at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the monument to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky looks too bright. Portrait mode is not needed here; the default photo mode keeps the whole scene sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters outdoor monuments and reduces harsh shadows, but any clear time of day works for a quick photo.
